title: A contact path for a small clinic
metaTitle: A small clinic contact page that books the visit
excerpt: Tell an anxious patient what happens after they reach the clinic, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to book a visit. A ten-field form is how you lose them.
alt: A cream sofa between two bright windows, with a framed abstract painting and teal vases, a room set up for a conversation, for a contact path that should feel like a clear next step.
caption: A sofa between two windows. The next step should be this easy to see. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a clinic contact page include?
faqs.answer: A way to book a visit or call the desk, what happens after they do, how soon they hear back, and what to have ready. Include hours, the address, and any access limit such as steps. A map is useful after those sentences. A form alone, with no clock and no phone, leaves an anxious patient guessing.

faqs.question: How many fields can the form have?
faqs.answer: Enough to hold a slot or route a question, and no more. Name and phone number, plus the visit they want, are often enough for a first booking. Ask for history, insurance scans, and long descriptions after a person has confirmed, or in the room. Ten fields before a human reply is a reason people call a different clinic.

faqs.question: Should new patients and existing patients use the same form?
faqs.answer: No. A new patient needs a booking, while an existing patient may need to change a time, ask for records, or reach the desk about a problem. Label those doors. A single "Contact us" box mixes a cancellation with a file request, and the urgent note waits behind the wrong task.

markdown:
A small clinic contact page should tell a patient who is already anxious what happens after they reach out, how fast, and what to have ready. The action is to book a visit.

A form with ten fields is a way to lose them. They have already done the hard part, which is deciding to ask. The page should make the ask small, and the next hour predictable.

## Name the doors

A clinic has more than one kind of reach-out, and the page should show that without looking like a switchboard. Book a visit. Call the desk. Change or cancel a visit you already have. Ask for records, if that is a separate legal path. Each door gets a label a tired person can understand.

Do not merge them into "Contact us" and sort the inbox later. Later means a cancellation sits under a new-patient note over a weekend. Labeling is how the desk triages before anyone writes a novel. New patients see the booking first. Existing patients see the change and the records link without feeling they are in the wrong building.

Put hours, address, and the access sentence at the top, beside the doors. "Two steps at the entrance. Ring the bell." A patient who cannot do the steps needs to know before they fill anything in. A map can sit under the sentence. The sentence is what they can repeat to a driver.

If you are closed, say when you are next open, on the same screen. A contact page that looks available at midnight and is not will collect notes nobody sees until Thursday. Say that. People can wait when they know the wait. They panic when the form pretends a human is there.

## What happens after they book or write

The line under the button is the care. "The desk confirms by phone the same day, during open hours, and repeats the fee." "You will see a time on the screen if the slot is still free." "Records requests are answered by email within the period we state." Pick the true line. Different doors can have different lines. They should.

Name the role, not a private mobile number. "The front desk" is enough if the front desk is real. A patient wants to know a person owns the note. "We'll be in touch" does not name an owner. On a hard day, unnamed follow-up feels like being forgotten.

Show a confirmation on the screen, not only in an email. Repeat the visit type, the time if you have one, and what they should do if the email never arrives. Give them the phone number again. Email is an unreliable hallway in clinics. The screen is the receipt.

If you sometimes cannot take the visit, the path needs a no. Full diary. Wrong clinic. Needs urgent care elsewhere. Write the urgent redirect in calm words and put it where someone in the wrong place will see it before they celebrate a booking. A contact page must not complete a booking the clinic should not have offered.

## A clock you already keep

Publish the response time the desk hits on an ordinary week. Same day during open hours. Next morning if they write after close. Separate the clock for bookings, cancellations, and records if those queues move at different speeds. One "we respond promptly" covers none of them.

Do not promise instant confirmation because a template suggested it. Promise the diary you have. If online booking is live and reliable, say the time is confirmed when they see it. If a human still has to check, say the human checks before it is real. A false "you're booked" is a serious failure, not a small copy bug. People arrange work and pain around it.

State the timezone and the days. A patient from another town should not infer your Friday. If you do not read the form on weekends, the page should say so in the same size type as the button. Quiet honesty reduces the Monday pile of duplicates from people who wrote three times.

Match the clock to the voicemail. If the recording says "leave a message and we will call today" and the page says two business days, patients believe neither. One clock, both surfaces. Read them aloud at the desk before you publish a change.

## What to have ready, and what not to send

Tell them before the form, in a few lines, what makes the booking possible. The visit they want. A phone number that works today. A referral, if you require one. Whether to bring the insurance card to the visit rather than photographing it into a form.

Say what not to include. Full medical history in a web form. Photographs of an injury sent to a general inbox. Identity documents. Give the appropriate moment for those, which is often the visit itself or a channel your clinician has approved. A helpful patient will over-share if the page looks like it wants a case file. Protect them from that.

The list should match the services page. If that page said no referral, do not ask for one here. If that page named the visit "first visit," the form should use those words. Inconsistency at the door feels like the clinic is disorganized, and disorganization reads as unsafe when someone is anxious.

Preparation that is truly required, such as fasting or clothing, belongs on the visit page and again in the confirmation. It does not belong as a surprise checkbox in a contact form. People miss checkboxes. They should not miss a preparation that changes the visit.

## A short form that can be finished

For a new booking, four fields are plenty if the widget does not already have them. Name. Phone. The visit. A line for the reason, optional if the visit name is enough. Required fields marked in text. The button labeled "Book a first visit" or "Request a call," not "Submit."

When something is wrong, say what to fix beside the field and keep the rest. Move focus to the error or to the confirmation so a screen reader hears the result. Do not use color as the only signal. Do not time out the form and wipe it while someone is looking for their insurance number in another room.

WCAG 2 groups this under four principles: perceivable, operable, understandable, and robust. The W3C overview is explicit that the guidelines cover forms and mobile content, not only articles. Labels, instructions, and errors a person can understand are the understandable part. A control that works with a thumb or a keyboard is the operable part. A clinic form that fails those basics fails the patient who most needs a straightforward door.

Do not pre-check a newsletter box. Do not force an account with a password before they can ask for a visit. An account may be useful for existing patients. It is a wall for new ones. Offer it after they are in the book, if at all.

Captcha and aggressive spam tools should not sit on the only door. If you are being flooded, fix routing and use a quieter control. A patient in pain will not fight a puzzle to reach a desk.

## Where the path has to agree

The homepage, the visit blocks, the fee, and this page should use one verb. Book a visit. Landing from a knee-pain block should open a knee-pain booking, or a form that already says that is the visit. Making them reselect from a departmental list restarts the doubt your services page just resolved.

Cancellations need a path that does not look like a new booking. People will otherwise make a second appointment to avoid figuring out how to undo the first. Put "Change or cancel" in the footer and on the confirmation. Tell them the notice you need, the same notice as the pricing page.

Keep a fallback when the widget breaks. A visible phone number and a named email the desk actually reads. A contact page that is only a script is a closed clinic on the day the script fails. Write the fallback in text. Test it monthly by using it yourself, on a phone, after hours, and see what the patient would see.

When you want the path designed as part of the site rather than glued on, book [an intro call](https://cal.com/hanabi/30min). Bring the diary rules and the voicemail script. The useful result is one clock and one set of doors.

## Review it like the desk

Once a month, book, cancel, and request a call from the public page. Check the screen, the email, and the queue. If the reply is slower than the promise, change the promise or the staffing. Do not leave a fantasy clock up because the layout was approved.

Read a week of notes. If patients are writing their history in the reason box, the prompt invited it or the services page failed to answer a fear. Fix the upstream page. The contact path should not become the place every unspoken question lands. It should be the booking.

When a staff member leaves, change any name on the page the same week. Role language ages better, and it still tells the patient a human exists. Store the routing rules with the other docs. On a Hanabi project that store is the client portal, next to the brand files, so a new desk lead inherits the clocks instead of inventing kinder ones the diary cannot keep.

The last edit, after the path is short, is to remove what the rest of the site still does to frighten or confuse. [What not to put on the site for a small clinic](/blog/what-not-to-put-on-the-site-for-a-small-clinic) is the cut list: stock smiles, procedure dumps, and the other additions that crowd out the room, the clinician, and this booking.
